source.text: לְמוֹאָ֡ב כֹּֽה־אָמַר֩ יְהוָ֨ה צְבָא֜וֹת אֱלֹהֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל ה֤וֹי אֶל־נְבוֹ֙ כִּ֣י שֻׁדָּ֔דָה הֹבִ֥ישָׁה נִלְכְּדָ֖ה קִרְיָתָ֑יִם הֹבִ֥ישָׁה הַמִּשְׂגָּ֖ב וָחָֽתָּה׃

records.literal_gloss: Concerning Moab. Thus says Yahweh of hosts, [the] God of Israel: Woe to Nebo, for it is devastated; is put to shame, is captured Kiriathaim; is put to shame the stronghold, and is shattered.

en.L: Concerning Moab. Thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of hosts, the God of Israel: Woe to Nebo, for it is devastated! \q Kiriathaim is put to shame, it is captured; \q the stronghold is put to shame and shattered.
en.B: Concerning Moab. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies, the God of Israel, says this: Woe to Nebo, for it lies in ruins! \q Kiriathaim is disgraced and captured; \q the stronghold is disgraced and shattered.
en.R: This message is about Moab. This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies, the God of Israel, says: How terrible it will be for Nebo! It is destroyed. \q Kiriathaim is captured, and its people are put to shame. \q The fortress is put to shame and torn down.

decisions.choice: Moab: the nation east of the Dead Sea; Nebo: one of its towns
decisions.reason: Chapter 48 is the oracle on Moab among the oracles on the nations (46-51). Moab lay east of the Dead Sea, between the Arnon and the Zered, and in this period held the plateau north of the Arnon as well. Nebo here is the town of that name (Numbers 32:3, 38), not the mountain. Much of the chapter takes up Isaiah 15-16, the earlier oracle on Moab, and the notes name those places.

decisions.choice: woe: a cry of grief and doom over Nebo
decisions.reason: The word is the cry of mourning used over the dead (22:18) and in the prophets over those facing judgment (22:13; 23:1; Isaiah 1:4).

decisions.choice: is devastated ... captured ... shattered: the fall pictured as already done
decisions.reason: The verbs are in the completed form, the way prophecy speaks of what is certain to come. Kiriathaim was a town of the plateau (Numbers 32:37; Joshua 13:19); with Nebo it is also named in the inscription of Mesha, king of Moab in the ninth century BC.

decisions.choice: the stronghold: a high, secure place, not a town's name
decisions.reason: The word means a height or refuge and is used of God as a stronghold (Psalm 46:8). With the article it most likely means Moab's fortress, or Kiriathaim's own citadel. Some take it as a place name, Misgab, since it stands among towns; no town of that name is known.

decisions.choice: disgraced (B); put to shame (R)
decisions.reason: The verb means both to be shamed and to be dried up or brought to nothing. Literal and Readable keep "put to shame"; Balanced uses "disgraced" for the same sense.

decisions.choice: This message is about Moab
decisions.reason: Readable turns the heading into a sentence and says "How terrible it will be" for "woe", as Isaiah and Jeremiah do elsewhere.

source.text: אֵ֣ין עוֹד֮ תְּהִלַּ֣ת מוֹאָב֒ בְּחֶשְׁבּ֗וֹן חָשְׁב֤וּ עָלֶ֨יהָ֙ רָעָ֔ה לְכ֖וּ וְנַכְרִיתֶ֣נָּה מִגּ֑וֹי גַּם־מַדְמֵ֣ן תִּדֹּ֔מִּי אַחֲרַ֖יִךְ תֵּ֥לֶךְ חָֽרֶב׃

records.literal_gloss: No more [is the] praise of Moab; in Heshbon they have planned against her evil: Come, and let us cut her off from [being a] nation. Also, Madmen, you will be silenced; after you will go [the] sword.

en.L: There is no more praise of Moab; \q in Heshbon they have planned evil against her: \q "Come, and let us cut her off from [being] a nation." \q You also, Madmen, will be silenced; \q after you the sword will go.
en.B: Moab's renown is gone. \q In Heshbon they have plotted disaster against her: \q "Come, let us wipe her out as a nation." \q You too, Madmen, will be silenced; \q the sword will pursue you.
en.R: No one praises Moab anymore. \q In Heshbon the enemy makes evil plans against Moab: \q "Come, let us destroy Moab, so that it is no longer a nation." \q The town of Madmen will also be silenced. \q Enemy soldiers will chase its people with swords.

decisions.choice: the praise of Moab: its renown, what it was praised for
decisions.reason: The word is used of the fame or glory of a city (49:25; 51:41). Moab's good name is over.

decisions.choice: in Heshbon they have planned: a play on the town's name
decisions.reason: Heshbon (Hebrew Cheshbon) sounds like the verb "plan" (chashevu): the town whose name means "reckoning" becomes the place where Moab's end is reckoned. Heshbon, Sihon's old city (Numbers 21:26), lay on Moab's northern edge; the enemy plots there, or takes it as a base. "They" are not named; the speech that follows shows that they are the invaders.

decisions.choice: Madmen, you will be silenced: a play on the town's name
alternatives: you will be utterly silenced (no town named)
decisions.reason: The name Madmen sounds like the verb "be silent" (damam), so the town is told it will live up to its name. The place is unknown elsewhere. Some suggest it is Dimon, a form of Dibon (Isaiah 15:9). The ancient Greek translation reads the words as a verb, "she will be utterly silenced", with no town named (a claim from general knowledge).

decisions.choice: come, let us cut her off: the words of the plotters
decisions.reason: The command and the "us" are the enemy's own words, quoted inside the oracle. "From being a nation" means that Moab will no longer exist as a people (compare Psalm 83:5).

decisions.choice: the enemy ... Enemy soldiers will chase its people with swords
decisions.reason: Readable names the plotters, which the Hebrew leaves unstated (m4), and explains "the sword will go after you".

source.text: ק֥וֹל צְעָקָ֖ה מֵחֹֽרוֹנָ֑יִם שֹׁ֖ד וָשֶׁ֥בֶר גָּדֽוֹל׃

records.literal_gloss: [The] sound of a cry from Horonaim: devastation and great destruction!

en.L: The sound of a cry from Horonaim: \q devastation and great destruction!
en.B: Listen! A cry from Horonaim: \q ruin and great destruction!
en.R: Listen to the cries from Horonaim! \q There is ruin and terrible destruction.

decisions.choice: the sound of a cry: listen, a cry
decisions.reason: "The sound of" at the head of a line often works as a call to listen (Isaiah 40:3, 6; Jeremiah 3:21).

decisions.choice: Horonaim: a town in the south of Moab
decisions.reason: Horonaim lay on the way down from the plateau toward the south (Isaiah 15:5; verses 5 and 34 below). It is also named in Mesha's inscription; its exact site is unknown.

decisions.choice: devastation and great destruction: a pair Jeremiah uses for total ruin
decisions.reason: The two words are the plunder of war and a crushing break (4:6, 20; 6:1; Isaiah 59:7; 60:18). They may be what the cry says, or describe what has caused it.

source.text: נִשְׁבְּרָ֖ה מוֹאָ֑ב הִשְׁמִ֥יעוּ זְּעָקָ֖ה צְעִירֶֽיהָ׃

records.literal_gloss: Is broken Moab; they have made heard a cry, its little ones.

en.L: Moab is broken; \q its little ones have made a cry heard.
en.B: Moab is shattered; \q its little ones cry out for all to hear.
en.R: Moab is broken. \q Its children are crying out loud.

decisions.choice: its little ones: the reading of the Hebrew text
alternatives: they have made a cry heard as far as Zoar
decisions.reason: The Hebrew is read as "its little ones", the children, or the humble and weak. The ancient Greek translation reads "to Zoar", from nearly the same letters, which would give "they have made the cry heard as far as Zoar" (compare verse 34; Isaiah 15:5). The Greek reading is given here from general knowledge.

decisions.choice: Moab is broken: the fall pictured as already done
decisions.reason: As in verse 1, the completed form speaks of the certain future. The verb "break" returns through the chapter (verses 17, 25, 38, 39).

source.text: כִּ֚י מַעֲלֵ֣ה הַלּוּחִ֔יתבִּבְכִ֖י יַֽעֲלֶה־בֶּ֑כִי כִּ֚י בְּמוֹרַ֣ד חוֹרֹנַ֔יִם צָרֵ֥י צַֽעֲקַת־שֶׁ֖בֶר שָׁמֵֽעוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: For [the] ascent of the Luhith, with weeping goes up weeping; for on [the] descent of Horonaim [the] distresses of [the] cry of destruction they have heard.

en.L: For [on] the ascent of Luhith \q with weeping, weeping goes up; \q for on the descent of Horonaim \q they have heard the anguish of the cry of ruin.
en.B: Up the climb to Luhith \q they go weeping, weeping all the way; \q on the way down to Horonaim \q they have heard the anguished cry of disaster.
en.R: People climb the hill to Luhith, \q weeping and weeping as they go. \q On the road down to Horonaim \q they hear the painful cries about the disaster.

decisions.choice: the ascent of Luhith, the descent of Horonaim: Isaiah 15:5 taken up
decisions.reason: The verse repeats Isaiah 15:5 with changes: Isaiah has "they go up it" where this verse has "weeping goes up" (one letter different), "the road to Horonaim" where this has "the descent of Horonaim", and "they raise a cry of ruin" where this has "they have heard the anguish of the cry of ruin". Both places lay on the route of flight to the south; their sites are unknown.

decisions.choice: with weeping, weeping goes up: weeping on weeping
decisions.reason: The doubled word stresses grief without end. The line may also be read "with weeping one goes up, weeping"; the sense is the same: the refugees weep all the way up the slope.

decisions.choice: the anguish of the cry of ruin: a cry full of distress
alternatives: the enemies have heard the cry of ruin
decisions.reason: The first word most likely means "distresses", so that the cry is an anguished one. The same letters can mean "enemies", giving "the enemies have heard the cry of ruin". The ancient Greek translation has no word for it (a claim from general knowledge), and Isaiah 15:5 has a different verb.

decisions.choice: Luhith: the reading of the Hebrew text
decisions.reason: The written letters here differ slightly from the name's spelling; the reading tradition gives Luhith, as in Isaiah 15:5.

decisions.choice: the climb to / the way down to
decisions.reason: Balanced follows the wording of Isaiah 15:5 ("Up the climb to Luhith") and gives the new word "descent" as "the way down".

source.text: נֻ֖סוּ מַלְּט֣וּ נַפְשְׁכֶ֑ם וְתִֽהְיֶ֕ינָה כַּעֲרוֹעֵ֖ר בַּמִּדְבָּֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: Flee, save your lives, and let them be like a juniper in the wilderness.

en.L: Flee! Save your lives, \q and be like a juniper in the wilderness!
en.B: Run! Save your lives! \q Be like a bare shrub in the wilderness!
en.R: Run away and save your lives! \q Live like a lonely bush in the desert.

decisions.choice: like a juniper in the wilderness: a lone shrub in dry land
alternatives: like a wild donkey in the wilderness
decisions.reason: The word names a desert shrub, perhaps a juniper, used in 17:6 for someone stripped and alone. The refugees will live like it, bare and cut off in the wilderness. The same letters spell Aroer, the town of verse 19, so some read "be like Aroer in the wilderness". The ancient Greek translation reads "like a wild donkey", from a word that looks similar (a claim from general knowledge).

decisions.choice: be: the verb is feminine plural
decisions.reason: The commands "flee" and "save" are masculine plural, but "be" is feminine plural. It may agree with "lives" (a feminine word): "let your lives be like a shrub". The sense is the same.

decisions.choice: a bare shrub
decisions.reason: Balanced uses the wording of 17:6 for the same shrub; Literal keeps "juniper".

decisions.choice: Live like a lonely bush
decisions.reason: Readable says what the picture means: the refugees will live alone in the desert like a single bush (m1).

source.text: כִּ֠י יַ֣עַן בִּטְחֵ֤ךְ בְּמַעֲשַׂ֨יִךְ֙ וּבְא֣וֹצְרוֹתַ֔יִךְ גַּם־אַ֖תְּ תִּלָּכֵ֑דִי וְיָצָ֤א כְמוֹשׁ֙ בַּגּוֹלָ֔ה כֹּהֲנָ֥יו וְשָׂרָ֖יו יַחְדָּֽיו׃

records.literal_gloss: For because you trusted in your works and in your treasures, also you will be captured; and will go out Chemosh into exile, his priests and his princes together.

en.L: For because you trusted in your works and in your treasures, \q you too will be captured; \q and Chemosh will go out into exile, \q his priests and his princes together.
en.B: Because you trusted in your achievements and your treasures, \q you too will be taken. \q Chemosh will go off into exile, \q together with his priests and his officials.
en.R: You trusted in the things you had done and in your riches. \q So you too will be captured. \q Your god Chemosh will be carried away to a foreign land, \q along with his priests and leaders.

decisions.choice: your works and your treasures: what Moab had made and stored up
decisions.reason: "Works" can mean deeds or the things a people has made, such as fortresses and cities; with "treasures" it means Moab's achievements and wealth. The ancient Greek translation reads "your strongholds" (a claim from general knowledge). Trusting in such things instead of God is a theme of Jeremiah (9:22; 17:5).

decisions.choice: Chemosh: the god of Moab
decisions.reason: Chemosh was the national god of the Moabites (Numbers 21:29; Judges 11:24). Solomon built him a high place near Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:7), which Josiah tore down (2 Kings 23:13). The written text spells the name slightly differently here; the reading tradition gives the usual form.

decisions.choice: Chemosh will go into exile: the god cannot save even himself
decisions.reason: Conquerors carried off the statues of defeated nations' gods with their priests and leaders (Isaiah 46:1-2; Jeremiah 43:12). The god Moab trusted is taken captive with the people. The line is close to Amos 1:15, said of Ammon's king, and Jeremiah 49:3 says it again of Milcom.

decisions.choice: princes (L); officials (B); leaders (R)
decisions.reason: The settled wording for this word (sar) in a court setting.

decisions.choice: Your god ... carried away to a foreign land
decisions.reason: Readable says who Chemosh is and what exile means (m2, m3).

source.text: וְיָבֹ֨א שֹׁדֵ֜ד אֶל־כָּל־עִ֗יר וְעִיר֙ לֹ֣א תִמָּלֵ֔ט וְאָבַ֥ד הָעֵ֖מֶק וְנִשְׁמַ֣ד הַמִּישֹׁ֑ר אֲשֶׁ֖ר אָמַ֥ר יְהוָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: And will come a destroyer to every city, and a city not will escape; and will perish the valley, and will be destroyed the plateau, as has said Yahweh.

en.L: And a destroyer will come against every town, and no town will escape; \q the valley will perish, and the plateau will be destroyed, \q as {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has said.
en.B: The destroyer will come upon every town; not one town will escape. \q The valley will be ruined and the plateau laid waste, \q just as {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} has said.
en.R: The enemy who destroys will attack every town. Not one town will escape. \q The valley will be ruined, and the high plain will be destroyed. \q {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} has said this will happen.

decisions.choice: the valley and the plateau: the two parts of Moab's land
decisions.reason: "The plateau" is the high tableland north of the Arnon, with towns such as Heshbon, Dibon and Medeba (verse 21; Deuteronomy 3:10; Joshua 13:9). "The valley" is most likely the Jordan valley below it, on the east side of the river (Joshua 13:27).

decisions.choice: a destroyer: the invading army
decisions.reason: The word is the same as in 6:26 and returns in verses 18 and 32. The destroyer is not named; in the setting of chapters 46-51 it is Babylon.

decisions.choice: The enemy who destroys
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that the destroyer is an enemy army (m2).

source.text: תְּנוּ־צִ֣יץ לְמוֹאָ֔ב כִּ֥י נָצֹ֖א תֵּצֵ֑א וְעָרֶ֨יהָ֙ לְשַׁמָּ֣ה תִֽהְיֶ֔ינָה מֵאֵ֥ין יוֹשֵׁ֖ב בָּהֵֽן׃

records.literal_gloss: Give wings to Moab, for flying away she will go out; and her cities a desolation will become, without inhabitant in them.

en.L: Give wings to Moab, \q for she will surely fly away; \q and her towns will become a desolation, \q with no one living in them.
en.B: Give Moab wings, \q for she must fly away; \q her towns will become a wasteland, \q with no one left living there.
en.R: Give Moab wings, \q because it must fly away. \q Its towns will become ruins, \q and no one will live in them.

decisions.choice: wings: the sense of the word is uncertain
alternatives: set up a gravestone for Moab
decisions.reason: The word usually means a flower or a shining plate (Isaiah 40:7; Exodus 28:36). Here, beside the verb "fly", it is most likely "wings" or "a wing": Moab must escape as a bird does. Other suggested senses are "salt", which an enemy spread on a ruined town so that nothing would grow (Judges 9:45), and "a gravestone" or marker. The ancient Greek translation reads "signs" (a claim from general knowledge).

decisions.choice: she will surely fly away: a doubled verb for emphasis
decisions.reason: A rare verb, "fly" (natsa), is joined to the common verb "go out" (yatsa), which sound alike; together they mean a sudden, certain flight. The rare verb also sounds like the noun of the first line.

decisions.choice: a desolation: an empty, frightening ruin
decisions.reason: The word is one of Jeremiah's for a land left waste, a horror to those who see it (2:15; 4:7; 25:11).

decisions.choice: it ... Its towns
decisions.reason: Moab is "she" in the Hebrew, as lands often are. Literal and Balanced keep "she"; Readable says "it".

source.text: אָר֗וּר עֹשֶׂ֛ה מְלֶ֥אכֶת יְהוָ֖ה רְמִיָּ֑ה וְאָר֕וּר מֹנֵ֥עַ חַרְבּ֖וֹ מִדָּֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: Cursed [is one who] does [the] work of Yahweh [with] slackness, and cursed [is one who] holds back his sword from blood.

en.L: Cursed [is] the one who does the work of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} with slackness, \q and cursed [is] the one who holds back his sword from blood.
en.B: Cursed is anyone who does the work of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} carelessly, \q and cursed is anyone who keeps his sword from shedding blood.
en.R: A curse on anyone who is lazy in doing {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}'s work! \q A curse on anyone who holds back his sword and does not use it!

decisions.choice: the work of the LORD: the judgment on Moab, carried out by its attackers
decisions.reason: The invaders are doing God's work when they strike Moab, as Babylon is God's servant in 25:9 and 27:6. A curse on one who holds back recalls Saul, who spared what God had given to destruction (1 Samuel 15:9, 23), and Ahab, who let Ben-hadad go (1 Kings 20:42). The saying does not praise violence in itself; it says the judgment will be carried out in full.

decisions.choice: with slackness: half-heartedly or deceitfully
decisions.reason: The word means both slack, lazy work (Proverbs 10:4; 12:24) and deceit (Psalm 52:4). Here it is work done carelessly, without full effort.

decisions.choice: cursed ... cursed: a double curse formula
decisions.reason: "Cursed is the one who" is the form of the covenant curses (Deuteronomy 27:15-26; Jeremiah 11:3; 17:5). The verse is prose-like in length, but the accents divide it into two parallel halves and it is set in lines with the rest of the poem.

decisions.choice: A curse on anyone ... does not use it
decisions.reason: Readable puts the curse as an exclamation and says "does not use it" for "holds back from blood".

source.text: שַׁאֲנַ֨ן מוֹאָ֜ב מִנְּעוּרָ֗יו וְשֹׁקֵ֥ט הוּא֙ אֶל־שְׁמָרָ֔יו וְלֹֽא־הוּרַ֤ק מִכְּלִי֙ אֶל־כֶּ֔לִי וּבַגּוֹלָ֖ה לֹ֣א הָלָ֑ךְ עַל־כֵּ֗ן עָמַ֤ד טַעְמוֹ֙ בּ֔וֹ וְרֵיח֖וֹ לֹ֥א נָמָֽר׃ס

records.literal_gloss: At ease has been Moab from his youth, and undisturbed he [has been] on his dregs, and not has he been emptied from vessel to vessel, and into exile not has he gone; therefore has remained his taste in him, and his scent not has changed.

en.L: Moab has been at ease from his youth and has settled on his dregs; \q he has not been emptied from vessel to vessel, \q and into exile he has not gone; \q therefore his taste has remained in him, \q and his scent has not changed.
en.B: Moab has lived at ease since his youth, resting undisturbed on his dregs, \q never poured out from jar to jar, \q never carried off into exile. \q So his flavor has stayed in him, \q and his aroma is unchanged.
en.R: Moab has lived in peace since the nation began. It is like wine left to sit on its dregs. \q It has never been poured from one jar to another. \q It has never been taken away into exile. \q So it still tastes the same, \q and its smell has not changed.

decisions.choice: settled on his dregs, not poured from vessel to vessel: wine left undisturbed
decisions.reason: In winemaking the new wine was left on its lees, the sediment, for a time, then poured off into another jar to clear it. Wine left too long on the dregs grows thick and harsh. Moab is pictured as such wine: never disturbed, never purified by trouble, set in its ways. Zephaniah 1:12 uses the same picture for people "thickening on their dregs", sure that God will do nothing.

decisions.choice: his taste and his scent: Moab's character, unchanged
decisions.reason: The flavor and smell of the wine stand for what Moab is like. Because it has never been "poured out" in exile, its pride and complacency remain (verses 29-30). Verse 12 turns the picture into judgment: now it will be poured out.

decisions.choice: into exile he has not gone: Moab's long security
decisions.reason: Moab had been subdued by Israel's kings (2 Samuel 8:2; 2 Kings 3) and paid tribute to Assyria, but it had not been deported as Israel and Judah were.

decisions.choice: It is like wine left to sit on its dregs
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly that Moab is pictured as wine, which the Hebrew leaves to the image (m1).

decisions.choice: he, his
decisions.reason: Here the Hebrew speaks of Moab as "he", picturing the people as one man; Literal and Balanced keep "he", and Readable says "it".

source.text: לָכֵ֞ן הִנֵּ֖ה־יָמִ֤ים בָּאִים֙ נְאֻם־יְהוָ֔ה וְשִׁלַּחְתִּי־ל֥וֹ צֹעִ֖ים וְצֵעֻ֑הוּ וְכֵלָ֣יו יָרִ֔יקוּ וְנִבְלֵיהֶ֖ם יְנַפֵּֽצוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: Therefore look, days [are] coming, declares Yahweh, and I will send to him tilters, and they will tilt him, and his vessels they will empty, and their jars they will smash.

en.L: Therefore look, days are coming, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, \q when I will send to him pourers, and they will pour him out; \q they will empty his vessels \q and smash their jars.
en.B: So the days are coming, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, \q when I will send him men who tip out jars, and they will tip him out; \q they will empty his vessels \q and smash their jars to pieces.
en.R: So the time is coming, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, \q when I will send people to pour Moab out like wine. \q They will empty its jars \q and smash them to pieces.

decisions.choice: pourers, who pour him out: the picture of verse 11 turned to judgment
decisions.reason: The verb means to tip or tilt a vessel. Moab, the wine that was never poured, will be tipped out by men God sends: the invaders who take its people into exile. Breaking the empty jars means the land itself is wrecked.

decisions.choice: their jars: Moab's people seen as many
decisions.reason: "His vessels" and "their jars" both mean Moab's; the Hebrew moves from Moab as one man to its people as many. The ancient Greek translation reads "his jars" (a claim from general knowledge).

decisions.choice: days are coming: a time God has set
decisions.reason: The phrase introduces a coming act of God, in judgment or in rescue (7:32; 30:3).

decisions.choice: men who tip out jars
decisions.reason: Balanced explains the rare word for "pourers". Literal keeps "pourers".

decisions.choice: pour Moab out like wine ... empty its jars and smash them
decisions.reason: Readable says that Moab is pictured as wine and joins the two lines about the vessels and jars into one.

source.text: וּבֹ֥שׁ מוֹאָ֖ב מִכְּמ֑וֹשׁ כַּאֲשֶׁר־בֹּ֨שׁוּ֙ בֵּ֣ית יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל מִבֵּ֥ית אֵ֖ל מִבְטֶחָֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And will be ashamed Moab of Chemosh, just as were ashamed [the] house of Israel of Bethel, their confidence.

en.L: And Moab will be ashamed of Chemosh, \q just as the house of Israel was ashamed \q of Bethel, their confidence.
en.B: Moab will be shamed by Chemosh, \q as the house of Israel was shamed \q by Bethel, the god they relied on.
en.R: Moab will be ashamed of its god Chemosh, \q just as the people of Israel were ashamed \q of Bethel, the place of worship they trusted.

decisions.choice: ashamed of: disappointed and disgraced by what one trusted
decisions.reason: To be ashamed of a god is to find that it has failed, and to be shamed for having trusted it (2:36; Isaiah 1:29; 42:17). Chemosh will not save Moab (verse 7).

decisions.choice: Bethel, their confidence: the northern kingdom's shrine, or a god called Bethel
decisions.reason: Jeroboam set up a golden calf at Bethel for the northern kingdom (1 Kings 12:28-29), and Hosea says Israel will be ashamed of that calf (Hosea 10:5-6). When the north fell to Assyria (2 Kings 17), the shrine could not save it. Because Bethel stands beside Chemosh here, some take it as the name of a god, Bethel, known from later records of the region; either way it is the false object of Israel's trust.

decisions.choice: the house of Israel: the northern kingdom
decisions.reason: Here "the house of Israel" means the northern tribes, whose shrine was at Bethel and who had already gone into exile (3:6-8).

decisions.choice: the god they relied on
decisions.reason: Balanced takes "their confidence" as the god or shrine they trusted (m2); Literal keeps the bare word.

decisions.choice: its god Chemosh ... the place of worship they trusted
decisions.reason: Readable says that Chemosh is a god and that Bethel was a place of worship (m2).

source.text: אֵ֚יךְ תֹּֽאמְר֔וּ גִּבּוֹרִ֖ים אֲנָ֑חְנוּ וְאַנְשֵׁי־חַ֖יִל לַמִּלְחָמָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: How can you say, Warriors [are] we, and men of strength for battle?

en.L: How can you say, \q "We [are] warriors, \q and men of valor for battle"?
en.B: How can you claim, \q "We are warriors, \q strong men fit for battle"?
en.R: How can you say, \q "We are strong soldiers. \q We are brave men, ready to fight"?

decisions.choice: how can you say: a question that rejects the claim
decisions.reason: The question means "You cannot say this" (2:23; 8:8). "You" is plural: the fighting men of Moab, whose boast is quoted.

decisions.choice: men of valor: strong, capable fighting men
decisions.reason: The phrase can mean men of strength, ability or wealth; beside "for battle" it means seasoned soldiers.

source.text: שֻׁדַּ֤ד מוֹאָב֙ וְעָרֶ֣יהָ עָלָ֔ה וּמִבְחַ֥ר בַּֽחוּרָ֖יו יָרְד֣וּ לַטָּ֑בַח נְאֻ֨ם־הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ יְהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת שְׁמֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: Is devastated Moab, and [into] her towns he has gone up, and [the] choice of his young men have gone down to the slaughter, declares the King, Yahweh of hosts [is] his name.

en.L: Moab is devastated, and [into] her towns he has gone up, \q and the choicest of his young men have gone down to the slaughter, \q declares the King, \q {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of hosts [is] {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} name.
en.B: Moab is ruined, and the enemy has gone up into her towns; \q the finest of her young men have gone down to be slaughtered, \q declares the King, \q whose name is {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies.
en.R: Moab is destroyed, and the enemy has attacked its towns. \q Its best young men have gone down to be killed, \q says the King, \q whose name is {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} of Armies.

decisions.choice: her towns, he has gone up: the enemy has come up into Moab's towns
alternatives: her towns have gone up in smoke
the destroyer of Moab and its towns has come up
decisions.reason: The Hebrew is brief and unusual: the verb "has gone up" has no stated subject. Most likely the destroyer of verse 8 has come up against the towns (verse 18 has "the destroyer of Moab has come up"). It may also mean that the towns have gone up in smoke, or, with a small change, "the destroyer of Moab and of its towns has come up".

decisions.choice: the King, whose name is the LORD of hosts: the true king above Moab's king and god
decisions.reason: The title is used again in 46:18 and 51:57. Against Chemosh, who goes into exile (verse 7), and Moab's own king, the LORD is the King who rules the nations.

decisions.choice: gone down to the slaughter: killed like animals led to be slaughtered
decisions.reason: The picture is of a flock going down to the slaughter (11:19; 50:27; 51:40).

decisions.choice: the enemy
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the subject of "has gone up" (m1). Literal keeps "he".

source.text: קָר֥וֹב אֵיד־מוֹאָ֖ב לָב֑וֹא וְרָ֣עָת֔וֹ מִהֲרָ֖ה מְאֹֽד׃

records.literal_gloss: Near [is the] calamity of Moab to come, and his disaster hastens very [much].

en.L: The calamity of Moab is near to come, \q and his disaster hurries very fast.
en.B: Moab's downfall is close at hand; \q its disaster is rushing on.
en.R: Disaster will soon come to Moab. \q It is coming very quickly.

decisions.choice: near is the calamity, it hastens: words from the Song of Moses
decisions.reason: The line echoes Deuteronomy 32:35, "near is the day of their calamity, and what is prepared for them hastens", said of Israel's enemies. The word for calamity is used of the day of a nation's ruin (18:17; 46:21; 49:8).

decisions.choice: its disaster
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "his" for Moab, as the Hebrew has here; Balanced and Readable say "its".

source.text: נֻ֤דוּ לוֹ֙ כָּל־סְבִיבָ֔יו וְכֹ֖ל יֹדְעֵ֣י שְׁמ֑וֹ אִמְר֗וּ אֵיכָ֤ה נִשְׁבַּר֙ מַטֵּה־עֹ֔ז מַקֵּ֖ל תִּפְאָרָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: Mourn for him, all [who are] around him, and all knowing his name; say, How is broken [the] staff of strength, [the] rod of splendor!

en.L: Mourn for him, all who are around him, \q and all who know his name; \q say, "How the mighty staff is broken, \q the glorious rod!"
en.B: Grieve for him, all you his neighbors, \q all who know his fame; \q say, "How the mighty scepter is broken, \q the glorious staff!"
en.R: All you nations around Moab, mourn for it. \q All you who know how famous it was, grieve. \q Say, "Moab's mighty power is broken! \q Its glory is gone!"

decisions.choice: mourn: shake the head in sorrow
decisions.reason: The verb means to sway or shake the head, a gesture of grief and sympathy with those who suffer (15:5; 16:5; 22:10; Job 2:11).

decisions.choice: all who know his name: all who know of Moab's fame
decisions.reason: "Name" here is reputation. Those near and far are called to lament.

decisions.choice: the mighty staff, the glorious rod: the power of Moab's rule
decisions.reason: The staff is the rod a ruler holds, and so stands for kingly power (Psalm 110:2; Ezekiel 19:11-14). The two lines say the same thing twice: Moab's might and splendor are broken. "How" opens a lament, as in Lamentations 1:1.

decisions.choice: scepter
decisions.reason: Balanced says "scepter" for the first word, which means a royal staff here (m3), and "staff" for the second; Literal keeps "staff" and "rod".

decisions.choice: All you nations around Moab ... Moab's mighty power is broken
decisions.reason: Readable names who is called to mourn and says what the staff stands for (m3).

source.text: רְדִ֤י מִכָּבוֹד֙ וּשְׁבִ֣י בַצָּמָ֔א יֹשֶׁ֖בֶת בַּת־דִּיב֑וֹן כִּֽי־שֹׁדֵ֤ד מוֹאָב֙ עָ֣לָה בָ֔ךְ שִׁחֵ֖ת מִבְצָרָֽיִךְ׃

records.literal_gloss: Come down from glory, and sit in thirst, inhabitant, daughter of Dibon, for [the] destroyer of Moab has come up against you, he has ruined your strongholds.

en.L: Come down from glory and sit in thirst, \q inhabitant, daughter of Dibon; \q for the destroyer of Moab has come up against you, \q he has ruined your strongholds.
en.B: Come down from your glory and sit on the parched ground, \q you who live in Daughter Dibon, \q for Moab's destroyer has come up against you; \q he has torn down your fortresses.
en.R: People of Dibon, come down from your place of honor. \q Sit on the dry ground. \q The enemy who destroys Moab has come to attack you. \q He has torn down your strong walls.

decisions.choice: daughter of Dibon: the city and its people pictured as a woman
decisions.reason: As with "daughter of Zion", the city is spoken of as a woman. Dibon, north of the Arnon (Numbers 21:30; Isaiah 15:2), was a chief city of Moab; the inscription of Mesha king of Moab was found there.

decisions.choice: come down from glory, sit in thirst: from honor to humiliation
alternatives: sit in filth (with a small change)
decisions.reason: The city, once seated in honor, must come down and sit on the thirsty ground, as captives and mourners sat in the dust (Isaiah 47:1). "Sit" plays on "inhabitant", which is from the same verb: she who sits enthroned must sit in the dust. The written text has a slightly different form of "sit"; the reading tradition gives the command.

decisions.choice: the destroyer ... has ruined your strongholds
decisions.reason: The destroyer is the invader of verse 8. The verbs are in the completed form, as in a vision of what is certain.

decisions.choice: you who live in Daughter Dibon
decisions.reason: Balanced follows the wording "Daughter Zion" settled in Isaiah for such titles.

decisions.choice: People of Dibon ... your place of honor
decisions.reason: Readable explains "daughter of Dibon" as the city's people and "glory" as their place of honor.

source.text: אֶל־דֶּ֛רֶךְ עִמְדִ֥י וְצַפִּ֖י יוֹשֶׁ֣בֶת עֲרוֹעֵ֑ר שַׁאֲלִי־נָ֣ס וְנִמְלָ֔טָה אִמְרִ֖י מַה־נִּֽהְיָֽתָה׃

records.literal_gloss: By [the] road stand and watch, inhabitant of Aroer; ask [the] fleeing [man] and [the] escaping [woman]; say, What has happened?

en.L: Stand by the road and watch, inhabitant of Aroer; \q ask the man who flees and the woman who escapes; \q say, "What has happened?"
en.B: Stand by the road and keep watch, you who live in Aroer! \q Ask the man who is running and the woman who is escaping; \q ask them, "What has happened?"
en.R: People of Aroer, stand beside the road and watch. \q Ask the men and women who are running away, \q "What has happened?"

decisions.choice: Aroer: a town on the rim of the Arnon gorge
decisions.reason: Aroer stood on the north edge of the Arnon valley, on the main road (Deuteronomy 2:36; Joshua 13:9, 16). From there the people would see the refugees coming from the north.

decisions.choice: the man who flees and the woman who escapes: everyone in flight
decisions.reason: One verb is masculine and the other feminine, so the pair means all the refugees, men and women alike. The answer to the question comes in verse 20.

decisions.choice: the men and women who are running away
decisions.reason: Readable joins the pair into one phrase (m2).

source.text: הֹבִ֥ישׁ מוֹאָ֛ב כִּֽי־חַ֖תָּה הֵילִ֣ילוּ׀וּֽזְעָ֑קוּ הַגִּ֣ידוּ בְאַרְנ֔וֹן כִּ֥י שֻׁדַּ֖ד מוֹאָֽב׃

records.literal_gloss: Is put to shame Moab, for it is shattered; wail and cry out! Tell in [the] Arnon that is devastated Moab.

en.L: Moab is put to shame, for it is shattered; wail and cry out! \q Tell [it] by the Arnon \q that Moab is devastated.
en.B: Moab is disgraced, for it is shattered. Wail and cry out! \q Announce it by the Arnon: \q Moab is ruined!
en.R: Moab is put to shame and broken. Cry and wail! \q Tell the news beside the Arnon River: \q Moab is destroyed!

decisions.choice: Moab is put to shame ... wail: the refugees' answer, then a call to mourn
decisions.reason: The first words answer the question of verse 19. The commands to wail and cry out are plural in the reading tradition; the written text has them singular, addressed to the woman of Aroer. The sense is the same.

decisions.choice: the Arnon: the river gorge at the heart of Moab
decisions.reason: The Arnon runs west through a deep canyon into the Dead Sea (Numbers 21:13; Isaiah 16:2). News told there would spread through the whole land.

decisions.choice: the Arnon River
decisions.reason: Readable says that the Arnon is a river.

source.text: וּמִשְׁפָּ֥ט בָּ֖א אֶל־אֶ֣רֶץ הַמִּישֹׁ֑ר אֶל־חֹל֥וֹן וְאֶל־יַ֖הְצָה וְעַל־מֵיפָֽעַת׃

records.literal_gloss: And judgment has come to [the] land of the plateau, to Holon and to Jahaz and upon Mephaath,

en.L: And judgment has come to the land of the plateau, to Holon and to Jahaz and upon Mephaath,
en.B: Judgment has come on the land of the plateau: on Holon, Jahaz and Mephaath,
en.R: Judgment has come on the land of the high plain. It has come on Holon, Jahaz and Mephaath.

decisions.choice: verses 21-24: a list of the towns judged, set as prose
decisions.reason: The poem pauses for a list of towns on the plateau, all governed by "judgment has come". The accents give the list no parallel lines (verses 22 and 23 are each a single unit), so verses 21-24 are set as prose. The towns are named in no geographical order and end with "all the towns of the land of Moab" (verse 24).

decisions.choice: Holon, Jahaz, Mephaath: towns of the plateau
decisions.reason: Jahaz is where Israel defeated Sihon (Numbers 21:23); here the name has an ending meaning "to", as in Numbers 21:23. Mephaath was given to Reuben and became a Levite town (Joshua 13:18; 21:37); the written text spells it slightly differently. This Holon is known only here, not the town of Judah (Joshua 15:51).

decisions.choice: judgment: God's sentence carried out
decisions.reason: The word is used for a verdict and its execution. It returns in verse 47, "thus far the judgment of Moab".

decisions.choice: Jahaz
decisions.reason: The town keeps the form "Jahaz" used in verse 34, Isaiah 15:4 and Numbers 21:23.

source.text: וְעַל־דִּיב֣וֹן וְעַל־נְב֔וֹ וְעַל־בֵּ֖ית דִּבְלָתָֽיִם׃

records.literal_gloss: and upon Dibon and upon Nebo and upon Beth-diblathaim,

en.L: and upon Dibon, and upon Nebo, and upon Beth-diblathaim,
en.B: on Dibon, Nebo and Beth-diblathaim,
en.R: It has come on Dibon, Nebo and Beth-diblathaim.

decisions.choice: Dibon, Nebo, Beth-diblathaim
decisions.reason: Dibon and Nebo are named in verses 1 and 18. Beth-diblathaim is most likely the Almon-diblathaim of Numbers 33:46-47, a stopping place near Nebo; Mesha's inscription also names it.

decisions.choice: It has come on
decisions.reason: Readable repeats the verb in each verse of the list so that each is a full sentence.

source.text: וְעַ֧ל קִרְיָתַ֛יִם וְעַל־בֵּ֥ית גָּמ֖וּל וְעַל־בֵּ֥ית מְעֽוֹן׃

records.literal_gloss: and upon Kiriathaim and upon Beth-gamul and upon Beth-meon,

en.L: and upon Kiriathaim, and upon Beth-gamul, and upon Beth-meon,
en.B: on Kiriathaim, Beth-gamul and Beth-meon,
en.R: It has come on Kiriathaim, Beth-gamul and Beth-meon.

decisions.choice: Kiriathaim, Beth-gamul, Beth-meon
decisions.reason: Kiriathaim is named in verse 1. Beth-gamul is known only here. Beth-meon is the town called Baal-meon and Beth-baal-meon (Numbers 32:38; Joshua 13:17).

decisions.choice: It has come on
decisions.reason: As in verse 22.

source.text: וְעַל־קְרִיּ֖וֹת וְעַל־בָּצְרָ֑ה וְעַ֗ל כָּל־עָרֵי֙ אֶ֣רֶץ מוֹאָ֔ב הָרְחֹק֖וֹת וְהַקְּרֹבֽוֹת׃

records.literal_gloss: and upon Kerioth and upon Bozrah and upon all [the] towns of [the] land of Moab, the far and the near.

en.L: and upon Kerioth, and upon Bozrah, and upon all the towns of the land of Moab, the far and the near.
en.B: on Kerioth and Bozrah, and on all the towns of the land of Moab, far and near.
en.R: It has come on Kerioth and Bozrah, and on all the towns of Moab, far and near.

decisions.choice: Kerioth and Bozrah: towns of Moab
decisions.reason: Kerioth had a palace (Amos 2:2) and is named again in verse 41. This Bozrah is not the city of Edom (49:13); it is most likely Bezer on the plateau (Deuteronomy 4:43; Joshua 20:8).

decisions.choice: the far and the near: every town, without exception
decisions.reason: The pair of opposites means all of them (compare 25:26).

source.text: נִגְדְּעָה֙ קֶ֣רֶן מוֹאָ֔ב וּזְרֹע֖וֹ נִשְׁבָּ֑רָה נְאֻ֖ם יְהוָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: Is cut off [the] horn of Moab, and his arm is broken, declares Yahweh.

en.L: The horn of Moab is cut off, \q and his arm is broken, \q declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.B: Moab's horn is hacked off, \q and its arm is broken, \q declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.R: Moab's horn is cut off, and its strength is gone. \q Its arm is broken, and its power is ended, \q says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

decisions.choice: horn and arm: strength and power
decisions.reason: A horn is the strength of a wild ox or ram, and so of a people or king (1 Samuel 2:1; Psalm 75:11; Lamentations 2:3). The arm is power to act and fight (Psalm 10:15; Ezekiel 30:21). Both are broken: Moab can no longer defend itself.

decisions.choice: its strength is gone ... its power is ended
decisions.reason: Readable keeps the pictures and says what they mean (m1).

source.text: הַשְׁכִּירֻ֕הוּ כִּ֥י עַל־יְהוָ֖ה הִגְדִּ֑יל וְסָפַ֤ק מוֹאָב֙ בְּקִיא֔וֹ וְהָיָ֥ה לִשְׂחֹ֖ק גַּם־הֽוּא׃

records.literal_gloss: Make him drunk, for against Yahweh he has magnified himself; and will splash Moab in his vomit, and will become a laughingstock also he.

en.L: Make him drunk, \q for against {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} he has made himself great; \q and Moab will wallow in his vomit, \q and he too will become a laughingstock.
en.B: Make him drunk, \q for he has exalted himself against {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. \q Moab will wallow in his own vomit, \q and he too will become something to laugh at.
en.R: Make Moab drunk, \q because it has made itself proud against {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. \q Moab will roll in its own vomit, \q and people will laugh at it too.

decisions.choice: make him drunk: the cup of God's anger
decisions.reason: The command takes up the cup of wrath that the nations must drink in 25:15-29, where Moab is named (25:21), and they "drink and get drunk and vomit" (25:27). Drunkenness pictures helpless ruin and disgrace (13:13; 51:39).

decisions.choice: against the LORD he has made himself great: Moab's pride is defiance of God
decisions.reason: The verb means to make oneself great, to boast or act arrogantly against God (Psalm 35:26; Zephaniah 2:8, 10, said of Moab and Ammon). The reason is repeated in verse 42.

decisions.choice: wallow: splash or flounder
decisions.reason: The verb usually means to clap or strike the hands; here it pictures the drunkard falling and floundering in his own vomit.

decisions.choice: he too: Moab, who mocked others, will be mocked
decisions.reason: "He too" points ahead to verse 27: Moab laughed at Israel, and now Moab will be laughed at.

decisions.choice: something to laugh at
decisions.reason: Balanced uses an everyday phrase for "laughingstock"; Literal keeps the word.

source.text: וְאִ֣ם׀ל֣וֹא הַשְּׂחֹ֗ק הָיָ֤ה לְךָ֙ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אִם־בְּגַנָּבִ֖ים נִמְצָ֑א כִּֽי־מִדֵּ֧י דְבָרֶ֥יךָ בּ֖וֹ תִּתְנוֹדָֽד׃

records.literal_gloss: And was not the laughingstock to you Israel? Or among thieves was he found, that as often as your words about him you shook yourself?

en.L: And was not Israel the laughingstock to you? \q Or was he found among thieves, \q that whenever you spoke of him you shook your head?
en.B: Was not Israel a joke to you? \q Was he caught among thieves, \q that every time you spoke of him you shook your head in scorn?
en.R: Moab, did you not laugh at Israel? \q Was Israel caught with thieves? \q Every time you talked about Israel, you shook your head to mock it.

decisions.choice: was not Israel ...? Or was he found ...?: questions that accuse Moab
decisions.reason: "You" is Moab. The first question means that Moab did mock Israel; the second asks whether Israel had done anything to deserve it, as if caught red-handed among thieves (2:26). The answer expected is no. Moab's scorn for Israel is condemned also in Zephaniah 2:8 and Ezekiel 25:8.

decisions.choice: you shook yourself: you shook your head in mockery
decisions.reason: Shaking or wagging the head was a gesture of scorn (18:16; Psalm 44:15; Lamentations 2:15). The verb is from the same root as "mourn" in verse 17, but here it is mockery.

decisions.choice: was he found: the reading of the Hebrew text
decisions.reason: The reading tradition has the masculine "he was found", for Israel; the written text has the feminine form. The sense is the same.

decisions.choice: Moab, ...
decisions.reason: Readable names the one addressed (m1).

source.text: עִזְב֤וּ עָרִים֙ וְשִׁכְנ֣וּ בַּסֶּ֔לַע יֹשְׁבֵ֖י מוֹאָ֑ב וִֽהְי֣וּ כְיוֹנָ֔ה תְּקַנֵּ֖ן בְּעֶבְרֵ֥י פִי־פָֽחַת׃

records.literal_gloss: Leave [the] towns and dwell in the rock, inhabitants of Moab, and be like a dove [that] nests in [the] sides of [the] mouth of [the] chasm.

en.L: Leave the towns and dwell in the rock, \q inhabitants of Moab; \q and be like a dove that nests \q in the sides of the mouth of a chasm.
en.B: Abandon the towns and live among the rocks, \q you people of Moab! \q Be like a dove that makes its nest \q in the cliffs beside the mouth of a gorge.
en.R: People of Moab, leave your towns. \q Go and live among the rocks. \q Be like a dove that builds its nest \q high on the sides of a deep canyon.

decisions.choice: like a dove nesting in the cliffs: hiding where the enemy cannot reach
decisions.reason: Rock doves nest in cracks high in canyon walls (Song of Songs 2:14). The people must leave their towns and hide in the rocks like them (compare 4:29).

decisions.choice: the sides of the mouth of a chasm: the walls at the opening of a gorge
decisions.reason: The last word means a pit or deep hole; it is the "pit" of verses 43-44. Here it is a ravine or gorge, such as the canyons that cut through Moab.

decisions.choice: the cliffs beside
decisions.reason: Balanced says "cliffs" for the "sides" of the gorge.

source.text: שָׁמַ֥עְנוּ גְאוֹן־מוֹאָ֖ב גֵּאֶ֣ה מְאֹ֑ד גָּבְה֧וֹ וּגְאוֹנ֛וֹ וְגַאֲוָת֖וֹ וְרֻ֥ם לִבּֽוֹ׃

records.literal_gloss: We have heard [the] pride of Moab, proud very, his loftiness and his pride and his haughtiness and [the] height of his heart.

en.L: We have heard of the pride of Moab, very proud, \q its loftiness and its pride and its haughtiness and the height of its heart.
en.B: We have heard of Moab's pride, proud beyond measure: \q its lofty looks, its pride, its haughty airs, its heart held high.
en.R: We have heard how proud the people of Moab are. They are very proud. \q They look down on others. They think they are better than everyone, and their hearts are full of pride.

decisions.choice: we have heard of the pride of Moab: Isaiah 16:6 taken up
decisions.reason: Verses 29-30 repeat Isaiah 16:6 with additions. Isaiah lists three words for pride (haughtiness, pride, arrogance); this verse has four, adding "loftiness" and "the height of its heart", and moves "arrogance" and the empty boasts into verse 30. Piling up words from the same roots makes Moab's pride overwhelming. Zephaniah 2:10 also names Moab's pride.

decisions.choice: the height of its heart: arrogance
decisions.reason: A heart that is "high" is a proud mind that looks down on others and on God (Deuteronomy 8:14; Ezekiel 31:10).

decisions.choice: we: the speaker and those with him
decisions.reason: As in Isaiah 16:6, "we" may be the prophet with his people; in verse 30 the LORD speaks.

decisions.choice: the wording of Isaiah 16:6
decisions.reason: Each level keeps its Isaiah 16:6 wording for the words the two verses share (Literal "haughtiness ... pride", Balanced "haughty airs ... pride", Readable "how proud ... think they are better than everyone") and adds the new words. As in Isaiah, Literal and Balanced say "its" for the Hebrew "his", meaning Moab.

source.text: אֲנִ֤י יָדַ֨עְתִּי֙נְאֻם־יְהוָ֔ה עֶבְרָת֖וֹ וְלֹא־כֵ֑ן בַּדָּ֖יו לֹא־כֵ֥ן עָשֽׂוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: I know, declares Yahweh, his arrogance, and not right; his empty boasts, not right have they done.

en.L: I myself know, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, its arrogance, and [it is] not right; \q its empty boasts, not right [is what] they have done.
en.B: I know its overbearing fury, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}; it is hollow. \q Its big talk comes to nothing, and nothing they do turns out right.
en.R: I know how arrogant and angry they are, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. But it is all empty. \q Their boasting is empty, and what they do comes to nothing.

decisions.choice: its arrogance, not right, its empty boasts: the end of Isaiah 16:6
decisions.reason: The words "its arrogance ... not right its empty boasts" are the last line of Isaiah 16:6. Here they are spoken by the LORD ("I know"), and a further "not right they have done" is added.

decisions.choice: arrogance: overflowing insolence or fury
decisions.reason: The word means pride that overflows its banks, and also rage (Isaiah 16:6, the note there).

decisions.choice: not right ... not right: Moab's boasting is empty and its deeds come to nothing
alternatives: what they have done is wrong
decisions.reason: "Not so" means not true or not sound. Moab's boasts are hollow, and its actions accomplish nothing, or are not as they should be.

decisions.choice: I know: God himself has seen Moab's pride
decisions.reason: The pronoun "I" is stated, which stresses the speaker: no boast is hidden from the LORD.

decisions.choice: overbearing fury ... big talk
decisions.reason: Balanced uses its wording from Isaiah 16:6 for the shared words.

source.text: עַל־כֵּן֙ עַל־מוֹאָ֣ב אֲיֵלִ֔יל וּלְמוֹאָ֥ב כֻּלֹּ֖ה אֶזְעָ֑ק אֶל־אַנְשֵׁ֥י קִֽיר־חֶ֖רֶשׂ יֶהְגֶּֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: Therefore over Moab I will wail, and for Moab, all of it, I will cry out; for [the] men of Kir-heres one moans.

en.L: Therefore over Moab I will wail, \q and for Moab, all of it, I will cry out; \q for the men of Kir-heres one moans.
en.B: So I wail over Moab; \q for all Moab I cry out; \q for the men of Kir-heres there is moaning.
en.R: So I cry over Moab. \q I cry out for all the people of Moab. \q People moan for the men of Kir-heres.

decisions.choice: wail for Moab, moan for Kir-heres: Isaiah 16:7 taken up
decisions.reason: Isaiah 16:7 says "Moab will wail for Moab ... for the raisin cakes of Kir-hareseth you will moan". Here the speaker himself wails ("I will wail"), and the grief is for "the men of Kir-heres", not its raisin cakes. Kir-heres is the shorter form of Kir-hareseth, used in Isaiah 16:11 and in verse 36; it is Moab's capital, Kir of Moab (Isaiah 15:1; 2 Kings 3:25).

decisions.choice: I will wail ... I will cry out: the speaker mourns for Moab
decisions.reason: The speaker is not named. Just before, the LORD speaks (verse 30), and in verse 33 the LORD says "I have made the wine cease"; so the grief may be God's own, or the prophet's, as in Isaiah 15:5 and 16:9-11. The text does not settle it.

decisions.choice: one moans: the third person in the Hebrew text
alternatives: I moan for the men of Kir-heres
decisions.reason: The verb is "he moans", with no subject named, which may mean "one moans" or "there is moaning". With the change of one letter it would be "I moan", matching the first two lines; some ancient translations read it that way (a claim from general knowledge).

decisions.choice: there is moaning (B); People moan (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable express the unnamed subject of "he moans" (m3) without choosing who it is.

source.text: מִבְּכִ֨י יַעְזֵ֤ר אֶבְכֶּה־לָּךְ֙ הַגֶּ֣פֶן שִׂבְמָ֔ה נְטִֽישֹׁתַ֨יִךְ֙ עָ֣בְרוּ יָ֔ם עַ֛ד יָ֥ם יַעְזֵ֖ר נָגָ֑עוּ עַל־קֵיצֵ֥ךְ וְעַל־בְּצִירֵ֖ךְ שֹׁדֵ֥דנָפָֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: More than [the] weeping of Jazer I weep for you, the vine of Sibmah; your shoots crossed over [the] sea, to [the] sea of Jazer they reached; upon your summer fruit and upon your vintage a destroyer has fallen.

en.L: More than the weeping of Jazer I weep for you, vine of Sibmah; \q your shoots crossed over [the] sea, \q to the sea of Jazer they reached; \q on your summer fruit and on your vintage the destroyer has fallen.
en.B: More than Jazer weeps, I weep for you, vine of Sibmah. \q Your runners crossed the sea \q and reached as far as the sea of Jazer. \q On your summer fruit and your grape harvest the destroyer has fallen.
en.R: Vine of Sibmah, I cry for you even more than the people of Jazer cry. \q Your branches spread across the Dead Sea. \q They reached as far as the sea of Jazer. \q But the destroyer has attacked your ripe fruit and your grapes.

decisions.choice: the vine of Sibmah: Isaiah 16:8-9 taken up
decisions.reason: The verse joins parts of Isaiah 16:8 and 16:9. Isaiah says "I weep with the weeping of Jazer"; this verse says "more than the weeping of Jazer" and speaks to the vine directly ("for you"). Isaiah's shoots "reached to Jazer ... crossed the sea"; here they "crossed the sea, reached to the sea of Jazer". Isaiah's last line has "the shout has fallen" on the harvest; here "the destroyer has fallen" on it, the reading Isaiah 16:9 notes as an alternative.

decisions.choice: the sea of Jazer: unknown, perhaps a copying slip
decisions.reason: No sea or lake is known at Jazer, a town north of Heshbon (Numbers 21:32). The word "sea" may have been written twice by a copyist, since it stands just before; Isaiah 16:8 has "to Jazer they reached". It may also name a pool or spring near the town.

decisions.choice: the sea, summer fruit and vintage
decisions.reason: The first sea is most likely the Dead Sea: Moab's vines, and their fame, spread far beyond its own land (Isaiah 16:8, note). Summer fruit is the ripe figs and grapes of late summer; the vintage is the grape harvest. The destroyer of verses 8 and 18 falls on it.

decisions.choice: I weep for you: grief for the enemy nation
decisions.reason: As in verse 31, the one who weeps may be the prophet or the LORD himself (verse 33).

decisions.choice: the Dead Sea
decisions.reason: Readable names the sea, as in Isaiah 16:8 (m3).

decisions.choice: shoots / runners / branches; vintage / grape harvest / grapes
decisions.reason: Each level follows its wording in Isaiah 16:8-9 for the shoots; for the new word "vintage" Balanced says "grape harvest".

source.text: וְנֶאֶסְפָ֨ה שִׂמְחָ֥ה וָגִ֛יל מִכַּרְמֶ֖ל וּמֵאֶ֣רֶץ מוֹאָ֑ב וְיַ֨יִן֙ מִיקָבִ֣ים הִשְׁבַּ֔תִּי לֹֽא־יִדְרֹ֣ךְ הֵידָ֔ד הֵידָ֖ד לֹ֥א הֵידָֽד׃

records.literal_gloss: And are gathered away gladness and joy from [the] fruitful land and from [the] land of Moab; and wine from [the] presses I have made to cease; not will tread [with] shouting; [the] shouting [is] not shouting.

en.L: And gladness and joy are gathered away from the fruitful land and from the land of Moab; \q and wine from the presses I have made to cease; \q no one treads with shouting; \q the shouting [is] no shouting.
en.B: Gladness and delight are gathered up and gone from the garden land, from the land of Moab. \q I have stopped the wine from flowing from the presses; \q no one treads the grapes with the harvest shout. \q The shouting is no shout of joy.
en.R: There is no more joy or gladness in the orchards or anywhere in Moab. \q I have stopped the wine from flowing from the winepresses. \q No one crushes the grapes with happy shouts. \q The shouting people hear is not a happy shout.

decisions.choice: gladness and joy gathered away: Isaiah 16:10 taken up
decisions.reason: The verse follows Isaiah 16:10 with changes: it adds "and from the land of Moab", leaves out the line about singing in the vineyards, and says "wine from the presses I have made to cease" where Isaiah has "the treader does not tread wine in the presses ... the shout I have made to cease". It ends with a new line: "the shouting is no shouting".

decisions.choice: the shouting is no shouting: the harvest cry has become a battle cry
decisions.reason: The word is the rhythmic shout of the grape treaders (25:30). The shout now heard in Moab is not the joy of harvest but the war cry of the enemy (compare 51:14, where the same word is the shout of victors).

decisions.choice: the fruitful land: orchard and garden country
decisions.reason: The word is the same as the name Carmel, but here it means fertile land with fruit trees and vines, as in Isaiah 16:10.

decisions.choice: I have made to cease: God speaks
decisions.reason: The LORD himself has ended the joy of the harvest, as in Isaiah 16:10. Verse 35 continues, "I will make an end".

decisions.choice: the wording of Isaiah 16:10
decisions.reason: Each level keeps its Isaiah 16:10 wording for the shared lines (Literal "gathered away from the fruitful land", Balanced "gathered up and gone from the garden land", Readable "no more joy or gladness in the orchards").

source.text: מִזַּעֲקַ֨ת חֶשְׁבּ֜וֹן עַד־אֶלְעָלֵ֗ה עַד־יַ֨הַץ֙ נָתְנ֣וּ קוֹלָ֔ם מִצֹּ֨עַר֙ עַד־חֹ֣רֹנַ֔יִם עֶגְלַ֖ת שְׁלִֽשִׁיָּ֑ה כִּ֚י גַּם־מֵ֣י נִמְרִ֔ים לִמְשַׁמּ֖וֹת יִהְיֽוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: From [the] cry of Heshbon to Elealeh, to Jahaz they have given their voice, from Zoar to Horonaim, Eglath-shelishiyah; for also [the] waters of Nimrim desolations will become.

en.L: From the cry of Heshbon as far as Elealeh, as far as Jahaz, they have raised their voice, \q from Zoar as far as Horonaim, Eglath-shelishiyah; \q for even the waters of Nimrim will become desolations.
en.B: The cry of Heshbon is heard in Elealeh; they raise their voices as far as Jahaz, \q from Zoar to Horonaim and Eglath-shelishiyah. \q Even the waters of Nimrim will turn to waste ground.
en.R: The people of Heshbon cry out, and their cries are heard in Elealeh and as far away as Jahaz. \q People cry from Zoar all the way to Horonaim and Eglath-shelishiyah. \q Even the streams at Nimrim will become dry land.

decisions.choice: Heshbon to Jahaz, Zoar, Eglath-shelishiyah, Nimrim: Isaiah 15:4-6 taken up
decisions.reason: The verse gathers phrases from Isaiah 15:4 ("Heshbon cries out, and Elealeh; as far as Jahaz their voice is heard"), 15:5 ("as far as Zoar, Eglath-shelishiyah") and 15:6 ("the waters of Nimrim are desolations"). It adds Horonaim from 15:5 and has "they have given their voice" for "their voice is heard", and "will become" for "are". The places run from Heshbon in the north to Zoar in the far south: the cry fills the land.

decisions.choice: from the cry of Heshbon ... they have raised their voice
decisions.reason: The Hebrew is compressed: the cry starts at Heshbon and is taken up town after town. The first phrase may also mean "because of the cry of Heshbon".

decisions.choice: Eglath-shelishiyah, Nimrim
decisions.reason: As in Isaiah 15:5-6: Eglath-shelishiyah is otherwise unknown (the name may mean "the third Eglath"), and the waters of Nimrim are most likely a stream in the south of Moab.

decisions.choice: is heard
decisions.reason: Balanced supplies a verb for the first phrase, as Isaiah 15:4 has "is heard".

decisions.choice: waste ground / dry land
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable keep their Isaiah 15:6 wording.

source.text: וְהִשְׁבַּתִּ֥י לְמוֹאָ֖ב נְאֻם־יְהוָ֑ה מַעֲלֶ֣ה בָמָ֔ה וּמַקְטִ֖יר לֵאלֹהָֽיו׃

records.literal_gloss: And I will make cease for Moab, declares Yahweh, [one] offering up [at the] high place and burning incense to his gods.

en.L: And I will make an end in Moab, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, \q of the one who offers up [sacrifice at] the high place \q and burns incense to {{gender:their|his}} gods.
en.B: I will put an end in Moab, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, \q to anyone who goes up to offer sacrifice at the high place \q and burns incense to {{gender:their|his}} gods.
en.R: I will stop the people of Moab, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, \q from offering sacrifices at their hilltop shrines \q and burning incense to their gods.

decisions.choice: the high place: a hilltop shrine
decisions.reason: High places were open-air shrines on hills where sacrifices and incense were offered (7:31; Isaiah 15:2; 16:12). Moab weeps and prays at its high place in Isaiah 16:12, to no effect; here God ends that worship altogether.

decisions.choice: the one who offers ... to his gods: every worshiper
decisions.reason: The singular participles mean anyone who worships there. "His gods" may also be "his god", Chemosh, since the word for God is plural in form.

decisions.choice: their, with "his" as the alternative
decisions.reason: The worshiper stands for anyone, man or woman, so the pronoun follows the gender setting.

decisions.choice: hilltop shrines
decisions.reason: Readable explains "high place" (m1) and speaks of Moab's people as a whole.

source.text: עַל־כֵּ֞ן לִבִּ֤י לְמוֹאָב֙ כַּחֲלִלִ֣ים יֶהֱמֶ֔ה וְלִבִּי֙ אֶל־אַנְשֵׁ֣י קִֽיר־חֶ֔רֶשׂ כַּחֲלִילִ֖ים יֶהֱמֶ֑ה עַל־כֵּ֛ן יִתְרַ֥ת עָשָׂ֖ה אָבָֽדוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: Therefore my heart for Moab like flutes moans, and my heart for [the] men of Kir-heres like flutes moans; therefore [the] abundance [that] it gained has perished.

en.L: Therefore my heart moans for Moab like flutes, \q and my heart moans for the men of Kir-heres like flutes; \q therefore the abundance [that] it has gained has perished.
en.B: So my heart moans for Moab like a flute; \q my heart moans like a flute for the men of Kir-heres. \q So the riches they had amassed are lost.
en.R: My heart is sad for Moab. It cries like the sad music of a flute. \q My heart mourns like a flute for the men of Kir-heres. \q All the riches they had saved are gone.

decisions.choice: my heart moans like flutes: Isaiah 16:11 and 15:7 taken up
decisions.reason: Isaiah 16:11 has "my inward parts sound like a lyre for Moab, and my inner being for Kir-heres". Here the speaker's heart moans "like flutes", and the grief is for "the men of" Kir-heres. The last line takes up Isaiah 15:7, "the abundance it has gained", and adds "has perished".

decisions.choice: flutes: the pipes played at funerals
decisions.reason: The flute or reed pipe was played at feasts (Isaiah 5:12) and also at mourning (Matthew 9:23). Its low, wailing sound pictures the speaker's grief.

decisions.choice: the abundance it has gained has perished: the reason for the grief
decisions.reason: "It" is Moab; the verb "perished" is plural, for its many riches. Their wealth and stores are lost (compare verse 7).

decisions.choice: the riches they had amassed / All the riches they had saved
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable keep their Isaiah 15:7 wording for the shared phrase.

source.text: כִּ֤י כָל־רֹאשׁ֙ קָרְחָ֔ה וְכָל־זָקָ֖ן גְּרֻעָ֑ה עַ֤ל כָּל־יָדַ֨יִם֙ גְּדֻדֹ֔ת וְעַל־מָתְנַ֖יִם שָֽׂק׃

records.literal_gloss: For every head [is] baldness, and every beard [is] cut short; upon all hands [are] gashes, and upon [the] loins sackcloth.

en.L: For every head [is] baldness, and every beard [is] cut short; \q on all hands [are] gashes, and on [the] loins sackcloth.
en.B: Every head is bald, every beard clipped short; \q there are gashes on every hand, and sackcloth around the waist.
en.R: All of them have shaved their heads and cut off their beards to show their grief. \q They have cut their hands, and they wear rough sackcloth around their waists.

decisions.choice: every head bald, every beard cut: Isaiah 15:2-3 taken up
decisions.reason: The first line is Isaiah 15:2 ("on all its heads is baldness, every beard is cut short") with "every head" for "all its heads". The sackcloth comes from Isaiah 15:3; the gashes on the hands are new.

decisions.choice: shaved heads, cut beards, gashes, sackcloth: signs of mourning
decisions.reason: Mourners shaved the head, cut the beard, gashed their skin and wore rough sackcloth (16:6; 41:5; 47:5). Israel's law forbade cutting the body for the dead (Leviticus 19:28; Deuteronomy 14:1), but Moab mourned in this way.

decisions.choice: to show their grief ... rough
decisions.reason: Readable keeps its Isaiah 15:2-3 wording and says why they do this (m2).

source.text: עַ֣ל כָּל־גַּגּ֥וֹת מוֹאָ֛ב וּבִרְחֹבֹתֶ֖יהָ כֻּלֹּ֣ה מִסְפֵּ֑ד כִּֽי־שָׁבַ֣רְתִּי אֶת־מוֹאָ֗ב כִּכְלִ֛י אֵֽין־חֵ֥פֶץ בּ֖וֹ נְאֻם־יְהוָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: Upon all [the] roofs of Moab and in its squares, all of it [is] lamentation; for I have broken Moab like a vessel [in which there is] no delight, declares Yahweh.

en.L: On all the roofs of Moab and in its squares, all of it [is] lamentation; \q for I have broken Moab like a vessel no one delights in, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.B: On all the roofs of Moab and in its open squares there is nothing but mourning, \q for I have smashed Moab like a jar that no one wants, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.R: On every flat roof in Moab and in its town squares there is only weeping. \q I have broken Moab like a jar that no one wants anymore, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

decisions.choice: on its roofs and in its squares: Isaiah 15:3 taken up
decisions.reason: Isaiah 15:3 has "on its roofs and in its squares all of it wails"; here "all of it is lamentation". Houses had flat roofs where people could lament in public.

decisions.choice: like a vessel no one delights in: thrown away as worthless
decisions.reason: The same phrase is said of King Coniah in 22:28 (compare Hosea 8:8). A clay jar no one wants is smashed and thrown out (19:11). The LORD has broken Moab.

decisions.choice: the wording of 22:28
decisions.reason: Each level uses its wording from 22:28 for the shared phrase.

source.text: אֵ֥יךְ חַ֨תָּה֙ הֵילִ֔ילוּ אֵ֛יךְ הִפְנָה־עֹ֥רֶף מוֹאָ֖ב בּ֑וֹשׁ וְהָיָ֥ה מוֹאָ֛ב לִשְׂחֹ֥ק וְלִמְחִתָּ֖ה לְכָל־סְבִיבָֽיו׃ס

records.literal_gloss: How it is shattered! They wail! How has turned [the] back Moab in shame! And will become Moab a laughingstock and a terror to all around him.

en.L: How it is shattered! They wail! \q How Moab has turned [its] back in shame! \q And Moab will become a laughingstock and a horror to all around him.
en.B: How shattered it is! How they wail! \q How Moab has turned its back in shame! \q Moab will become something to laugh at and a thing of horror to all its neighbors.
en.R: Moab is broken! Hear how its people wail! \q Moab has turned and run away in shame. \q All the nations around it will laugh at it and be horrified by what has happened to it.

decisions.choice: how it is shattered! they wail!: a lament
decisions.reason: "How" opens a cry of lament, as in verse 17. "They wail" may also be a command, "Wail!", as in verse 20; the form is the same.

decisions.choice: turned its back: fled in defeat
decisions.reason: To turn the back is to run from the enemy (Joshua 7:8, 12). Moab's warriors, who boasted in verse 14, flee in shame.

decisions.choice: a laughingstock and a horror: mocked and dreaded
decisions.reason: Moab becomes the laughingstock it made of Israel (verses 26-27), and also a terror: its neighbors are frightened by its fall.

decisions.choice: Hear how its people wail ... All the nations around it
decisions.reason: Readable supplies the subjects the Hebrew leaves unstated.

source.text: כִּי־כֹה֙ אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה הִנֵּ֥ה כַנֶּ֖שֶׁר יִדְאֶ֑ה וּפָרַ֥שׂ כְּנָפָ֖יו אֶל־מוֹאָֽב׃

records.literal_gloss: For thus says Yahweh: Look, like the eagle he will swoop, and he will spread his wings against Moab.

en.L: For thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}: \q Look, like an eagle he will swoop down \q and spread his wings against Moab.
en.B: For {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says this: \q Look! Like an eagle he swoops down \q and spreads his wings over Moab.
en.R: This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says: \q Look! The enemy will swoop down like an eagle \q and spread his wings over Moab.

decisions.choice: like an eagle he will swoop and spread his wings: the invader's sudden attack
decisions.reason: The bird may be an eagle or a vulture. The conqueror, Babylon's king, is pictured diving on its prey and covering it with its wings (4:13; Deuteronomy 28:49; Habakkuk 1:8). "He" is not named; it is the destroyer of the chapter, not the LORD.

decisions.choice: the same words return in 49:22, against Edom
decisions.reason: Verses 40b and 41b reappear almost word for word in 49:22, where they are said of Bozrah and Edom.

decisions.choice: the eagle lines: lacking in the ancient Greek translation
decisions.reason: The ancient Greek translation has "For thus says the LORD" but lacks the eagle line here and the line about the warriors' hearts in verse 41; it has them at 49:22 (in its own order). They may have been added here in the Hebrew from 49:22, or left out of the Greek because they appear there. This claim is given from general knowledge.

decisions.choice: The enemy
decisions.reason: Readable names the one pictured as an eagle (m1).

decisions.choice: over Moab
decisions.reason: The preposition can mean "to", "over" or "against". Balanced and Readable say "over", which suits wings spread over prey; Literal keeps "against".

source.text: נִלְכְּדָה֙ הַקְּרִיּ֔וֹת וְהַמְּצָד֖וֹת נִתְפָּ֑שָׂה וְֽ֠הָיָה לֵ֞ב גִּבּוֹרֵ֤י מוֹאָב֙ בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֔וּא כְּלֵ֖ב אִשָּׁ֥ה מְצֵרָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: Is captured the Kerioth, and the strongholds are seized; and will be [the] heart of [the] warriors of Moab in that day like [the] heart of a woman in labor.

en.L: Kerioth is captured, \q and the strongholds are seized; \q and the heart of the warriors of Moab on that day will be \q like the heart of a woman in labor.
en.B: Kerioth is taken, \q the strongholds are seized. \q On that day the warriors of Moab will have hearts \q like the heart of a woman in labor.
en.R: Kerioth is captured. \q The forts are taken. \q On that day the soldiers of Moab will be terrified, \q like a woman giving birth.

decisions.choice: Kerioth: the town of verse 24, or "the towns"
decisions.reason: The word has the article, "the Kerioth". It is most likely the town named in verse 24 and Amos 2:2. It can also be the plural of the word for town: "the towns are captured".

decisions.choice: like the heart of a woman in labor: helpless terror
decisions.reason: As in 30:6 and 49:22, the pains of childbirth picture sudden, overwhelming fear. The warriors who boasted (verse 14) are shaken. 49:22 repeats this line of Edom's warriors (see verse 40).

decisions.choice: will be terrified, like a woman giving birth
decisions.reason: Readable says what the comparison means (m2).

source.text: וְנִשְׁמַ֥ד מוֹאָ֖ב מֵעָ֑ם כִּ֥י עַל־יְהוָ֖ה הִגְדִּֽיל׃

records.literal_gloss: And will be destroyed Moab from [being] a people, for against Yahweh he magnified himself.

en.L: And Moab will be destroyed from [being] a people, \q for against {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} he has made himself great.
en.B: Moab will be destroyed and no longer be a people, \q because he exalted himself against {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.R: Moab will be destroyed and will no longer be a nation, \q because it made itself proud against {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

decisions.choice: destroyed from being a people: Moab will no longer exist as a nation
decisions.reason: The phrase answers the plotters' words in verse 2, "let us cut her off from being a nation". The reason repeats verse 26.

decisions.choice: the wording of verse 26
decisions.reason: Each level repeats its wording of verse 26 for the same clause.

source.text: פַּ֥חַד וָפַ֖חַת וָפָ֑ח עָלֶ֛יךָ יוֹשֵׁ֥ב מוֹאָ֖ב נְאֻם־יְהוָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: Terror and pit and snare [are] upon you, inhabitant of Moab, declares Yahweh.

en.L: Terror and pit and snare \q [are] upon you, inhabitant of Moab, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.B: Fear and the pit and the trap \q are upon you who live in Moab, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.R: All of you who live in Moab, \q terror, a deep pit, and a trap are waiting for you, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

decisions.choice: terror and pit and snare: Isaiah 24:17 taken up
decisions.reason: Verses 43-44 repeat Isaiah 24:17-18. Isaiah speaks to "the inhabitant of the earth"; here it is "the inhabitant of Moab", and "declares the LORD" is added. The three Hebrew words sound almost alike (pachad, pachat, pach), so the line rings like an alarm.

decisions.choice: inhabitant of Moab: all who live there
decisions.reason: The word is singular but means the whole people, addressed together.

decisions.choice: the wording of Isaiah 24:17
decisions.reason: Each level keeps its Isaiah 24:17 wording, with Moab in place of the earth.

source.text: הַנָּ֞ס מִפְּנֵ֤י הַפַּ֨חַד֙ יִפֹּ֣ל אֶל־הַפַּ֔חַת וְהָֽעֹלֶה֙ מִן־הַפַּ֔חַת יִלָּכֵ֖ד בַּפָּ֑ח כִּֽי־אָבִ֨יא אֵלֶ֧יהָ אֶל־מוֹאָ֛ב שְׁנַ֥ת פְּקֻדָּתָ֖ם נְאֻם־יְהוָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: The [one who] flees from before the terror will fall into the pit, and the [one who] goes up from the pit will be caught in the snare; for I will bring upon her, upon Moab, [the] year of their punishment, declares Yahweh.

en.L: The one fleeing from before the terror will fall into the pit, \q and the one coming up from the pit will be caught in the snare; \q for I will bring upon her, upon Moab, the year of their punishment, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.B: Anyone who runs from the fear will drop into the pit, \q and anyone who climbs up out of the pit will be caught in the trap. \q For I will bring on her, on Moab, the year of their punishment, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.R: Anyone who runs away from the terror will fall into the pit. \q Anyone who climbs out of the pit will be caught in the trap. \q I will bring this on Moab when the time comes to punish them, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

decisions.choice: whoever flees falls into the pit: Isaiah 24:18 taken up
decisions.reason: Isaiah 24:18 begins "and it will be" and has "from the sound of the terror" and "from the midst of the pit"; this verse has "from before the terror" and "from the pit". In place of Isaiah's flood picture it ends with the year of Moab's punishment. Escaping one danger only leads into the next (Amos 5:19).

decisions.choice: the year of their punishment: the time set for their judgment
decisions.reason: As in 11:23 and 23:12, "year" means the appointed time when God deals with them.

decisions.choice: the one who flees: the reading of the Hebrew text
decisions.reason: The written text spells the word slightly differently; the reading tradition gives "the one who flees", as in Isaiah 24:18.

decisions.choice: the wording of Isaiah 24:18 and 11:23
decisions.reason: Each level keeps its Isaiah 24:18 wording where the Hebrew is the same, and its wording of 11:23 for "the year of their punishment".

source.text: בְּצֵ֥ל חֶשְׁבּ֛וֹן עָמְד֖וּ מִכֹּ֣חַ נָסִ֑ים כִּֽי־אֵ֞שׁ יָצָ֣א מֵחֶשְׁבּ֗וֹן וְלֶֽהָבָה֙ מִבֵּ֣ין סִיח֔וֹן וַתֹּ֨אכַל֙ פְּאַ֣ת מוֹאָ֔ב וְקָדְקֹ֖ד בְּנֵ֥י שָׁאֽוֹן׃

records.literal_gloss: In [the] shadow of Heshbon stand without strength fugitives; for fire has gone out from Heshbon, and flame from [the] midst of Sihon, and it has consumed [the] forehead of Moab and [the] crown of the head of [the] sons of tumult.

en.L: In the shadow of Heshbon fugitives stand without strength; \q for fire went out from Heshbon, and flame from the midst of Sihon, \q and it consumed the forehead of Moab \q and the crown of the head of the {{gender:children|sons}} of tumult.
en.B: In the shadow of Heshbon the fugitives stand, their strength spent, \q for fire went out from Heshbon, a flame from the midst of Sihon. \q It burned up the forehead of Moab, \q the skulls of the {{gender:people|sons}} of tumult.
en.R: The refugees stop in the shade of Heshbon. They have no strength left. \q But fire came out of Heshbon, flames from the city of Sihon. \q It burned up Moab's forehead \q and the heads of its proud, noisy people.

decisions.choice: fire from Heshbon, flame from Sihon: the song of Numbers 21:28 taken up
decisions.reason: Numbers 21:28 sings of the Amorite king Sihon's victory over Moab: "fire went out from Heshbon, flame from the town of Sihon; it consumed Ar of Moab". Here "from the midst of Sihon" stands for "from the town of Sihon", and the fire consumes "the forehead of Moab". The old victory song becomes a prophecy of Moab's fall again.

decisions.choice: the forehead of Moab and the skull of the sons of tumult: Balaam's oracle, Numbers 24:17
decisions.reason: Balaam said the star from Jacob "will crush the forehead of Moab and tear down all the sons of Sheth" (Numbers 24:17). This verse has "the crown of the head" for "tear down", a word that looks much the same, and "the sons of tumult" for "the sons of Sheth", which may be how the line was understood: Moab's noisy, boastful people or warriors.

decisions.choice: in the shadow of Heshbon the fugitives stand without strength: no refuge left
decisions.reason: Refugees stop exhausted in the shade of Heshbon, hoping for shelter; but fire comes out of the very city where they seek it. Heshbon, once Sihon's capital, was now in Moabite hands (verse 2).

decisions.choice: verses 45-47: lacking in the ancient Greek translation
decisions.reason: The ancient Greek translation ends the oracle with verse 44 and has nothing of verses 45-47. This claim is given from general knowledge.

decisions.choice: children / people of tumult, with "sons" as the alternative
decisions.reason: As in Numbers 24:17, "sons of" names a whole people, so the gender setting applies.

decisions.choice: flames from the city of Sihon
decisions.reason: Readable keeps its Numbers 21:28 wording; "the midst of Sihon" means Sihon's own city (m1).

source.text: אוֹי־לְךָ֣ מוֹאָ֔ב אָבַ֖ד עַם־כְּמ֑וֹשׁ כִּֽי־לֻקְּח֤וּ בָנֶ֨יךָ֙ בַּשֶּׁ֔בִי וּבְנֹתֶ֖יךָ בַּשִּׁבְיָֽה׃

records.literal_gloss: Woe to you, Moab! Has perished [the] people of Chemosh; for are taken your sons into captivity, and your daughters into captivity.

en.L: Woe to you, Moab! \q The people of Chemosh have perished; \q for your sons have been taken into captivity, \q and your daughters into captivity.
en.B: Woe to you, Moab! \q The people of Chemosh are destroyed. \q Your sons have been taken away as captives, \q and your daughters carried off into captivity.
en.R: How terrible it will be for you, Moab! \q The people who worship Chemosh are destroyed. \q Your sons have been taken away as prisoners, \q and your daughters too.

decisions.choice: woe to you, Moab, people of Chemosh: Numbers 21:29 taken up
decisions.reason: Numbers 21:29 has "Woe to you, Moab! You have perished, people of Chemosh! He has given his sons as fugitives, and his daughters into captivity". Here it is "the people of Chemosh have perished", and the sons and daughters "have been taken" captive, with no mention of Chemosh giving them up or of Sihon.

decisions.choice: woe: a cry of grief and doom
decisions.reason: The word here is a close relative of the cry in verse 1, said over those facing disaster (13:27; Numbers 21:29).

decisions.choice: the people of Chemosh: Moab, named by its god
decisions.reason: As in verse 7 and Numbers 21:29, Moab is called by the name of the god it served, who cannot save it.

decisions.choice: Woe to you (B); How terrible it will be for you (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable follow Jeremiah's wording for this cry (13:27) rather than Numbers 21:29, where Balanced has "How terrible for you".

source.text: וְשַׁבְתִּ֧י שְׁבוּת־מוֹאָ֛ב בְּאַחֲרִ֥ית הַיָּמִ֖ים נְאֻם־יְהוָ֑ה עַד־הֵ֖נָּה מִשְׁפַּ֥ט מוֹאָֽב׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And I will turn back [the] captivity of Moab in [the] latter part of the days, declares Yahweh. To here [is the] judgment of Moab.

en.L: Yet I will restore the fortunes of Moab in the latter days, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. Thus far [is] the judgment of Moab.
en.B: Yet I will restore the fortunes of Moab in days to come, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. Here ends the judgment on Moab.
en.R: But later on I will make things good again for Moab, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. This is the end of the message of judgment on Moab.

decisions.choice: restore the fortunes: turn ruin into well-being
decisions.reason: The same phrase as in 30:3 (see the note there), used of Israel and Judah, is here promised to Moab, as it is also to Ammon (49:6) and Elam (49:39). The judgment is not God's last word for the nation.

decisions.choice: the latter days: the time to come, after the judgment
decisions.reason: As in 23:20 and 30:24, the phrase means the later part of time, the future as seen from now.

decisions.choice: thus far the judgment of Moab: a closing note
decisions.reason: The last words close the oracle like a heading at its end, as 51:64 closes the words of Jeremiah. "Judgment" names the whole oracle on Moab. The verse is a prose ending to the poem and is not set in lines.

decisions.choice: restore the fortunes (L, B); make things good again (R); the latter days / days to come / later on
decisions.reason: The wording settled at 30:3 for "restore the fortunes", and each level's wording of 30:24 for "the latter days".
